claims.text: The transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition is driven by a percolating network of coherent ordered B2 precipitates.
A specific lattice misfit associated with the coherent B2 precipitates produces a dislocation-locking state at intermediate aging temperatures.
Ductility recovery at higher aging temperatures results from dislocation cross-slip or phase-boundary decohesion.
The initial alloy has a lamellar microstructure of alternating FCC and ordered B2 phases.
The FCC matrix initially has minimal pre-existing long-range chemical order.
Classical grain-boundary segregation is thermodynamically unfavorable or kinetically slow in the proposed aging regime.
The B2 phase remains coherent with the FCC matrix during the initial part of the aging regime.
Aging changes local chemical order within the FCC phase.
Aging changes the B2 phase-boundary morphology from a continuous coherent network to a discontinuous semi-coherent or incoherent network.
At intermediate aging temperatures, local chemical orders nucleate and grow within the FCC phase.
At intermediate aging temperatures, the B2 phase coarsens into a continuous coherent network.
Dislocations in the ordered domains must move in pairs as superdislocations to preserve chemical order.
Paired dislocation motion through the ordered domains produces order hardening and a dramatic loss of ductility.
Higher temperature enables superdislocation cross-slip or anti-phase-boundary formation that facilitates dislocation bypass.
Loss of phase-boundary coherency permits easier dislocation transmission and restores ductility.
Elongation to failure reaches a distinct minimum at the aging condition corresponding to the peak density of coherent ordered domains.
The ductility minimum is accompanied by a sharp increase in yield strength and a reduction in strain-hardening capacity.
The as-cast or solutionized state is moderately ductile because it lacks a percolating ordered network and its fine phase boundaries permit dislocation glide.
Embrittlement occurs while anti-phase-boundary energy is high enough to inhibit easy dislocation motion but low enough to permit stable ordered domains.

contradictions.description: Mechanical testing is specified at room temperature after aging, but recovery is partly attributed to thermal energy directly enabling cross-slip at the higher aging temperature. The hypothesis does not explain how this thermally activated mobility persists during subsequent room-temperature testing.

Phase-boundary decohesion is proposed as a cause of recovered ductility, whereas the mechanism elsewhere describes loss of coherency as enabling transmission or making boundaries more compliant. Interfacial decohesion denotes separation and is not equivalent to reduced coherency; it would ordinarily constitute a damage process rather than straightforwardly explaining ductility recovery.
